title: Massachusetts Oral Prescriptions: Receipt, Follow-Up and Emergency Dispensing
subtopic: Receipt duties, follow-up documentation, Failover and emergency dispensing
learning_objectives: Carry out the pharmacist's duties at the moment an oral controlled-substance prescription is received.
Choose the follow-up period from the route the prescription travelled, and identify who owes it.
Separate the Schedule VI Failover from an ordinary electronic-prescribing outage.

quick_review.text: On receiving an oral controlled-substance prescription the pharmacist must immediately reduce it to writing with the information Massachusetts requires, and must make a reasonable effort to authenticate a prescriber who is not known to the pharmacist.

The statutory default is an electronic follow-up prescription within 2 days; the 7-day written route is available only where the practitioner has RECEIVED an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner, and that follow-up duty does not reach Schedule VI.

Where the oral prescription for a Schedule II through V substance was issued under one of the enumerated electronic-prescribing exceptions, the regulation gives the practitioner not more than seven BUSINESS days and accepts either a written or an electronic prescription.

Most electronic-prescribing exceptions are categorical and are held by nobody: they attach to the prescription's circumstances, such as a veterinarian, a temporary technological failure, an emergency, or Schedule VI. Only a time-limited waiver is applied for and held.

A Failover is a Schedule VI device by definition: a document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, suffered a transmission defect, and was converted to a computer-generated facsimile. Only such a document counts as an oral prescription needing no follow-up.

In an emergency a pharmacist may dispense a Schedule II controlled substance on the practitioner's written or orally transmitted authorization, limited to the quantity adequate for the emergency period, with the practitioner owing a follow-up within seven business days.

decision_logic.condition: An oral controlled-substance prescription is received by telephone.
decision_logic.action: Reduce it to writing immediately with the required Massachusetts information, and authenticate the prescriber if that practitioner is not known to you.

decision_logic.condition: The prescriber has not received an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner.
decision_logic.action: Expect an electronic follow-up prescription within 2 days; the 7-day written route is not open to that prescriber.

decision_logic.condition: The oral Schedule II through V prescription was issued under one of the enumerated electronic-prescribing exceptions.
decision_logic.action: Expect a written or electronic follow-up within not more than seven business days, and treat a shorter federal period as controlling where one applies.

decision_logic.condition: The document began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, failed in transmission, and arrived as a computer-generated facsimile.
decision_logic.action: Only then consider the Failover route, and only if all three of its conditions hold and the drug is not an additional drug; otherwise the ordinary follow-up duty stands.

decision_logic.condition: A technological or electrical failure prevented electronic transmission of a Schedule II through V prescription.
decision_logic.action: That is the ordinary outage exception, not a Failover. The prescription may be issued orally or in writing, and the follow-up duty remains.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist dispenses a Schedule II controlled substance on oral authorization in an emergency.
decision_logic.action: Limit the quantity to the emergency period, reduce the prescription to writing at once, authenticate an unknown prescriber, expect the follow-up within seven business days marked Authorization for Emergency Dispensing, attach it on receipt, and notify the DEA if it never comes.

ma_vs_federal.text: For an emergency oral Schedule II prescription Massachusetts measures the practitioner's follow-up in seven BUSINESS days while the federal rule allows seven days from the oral authorization, so the federal period is the shorter one and controls.

Both Massachusetts follow-up provisions carry the qualifier that a shorter federally required period controls, and the federal period they point at is the seven days for an emergency oral Schedule II follow-up.

exceptions.text: Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement, and the statutory follow-up duty does not reach Schedule VI either.
A pharmacist receiving an otherwise valid written or oral prescription is not required to verify that it properly falls within an exception or waiver.

The three Failover conditions sit downstream of the definition. Meeting all three does nothing for a prescription that was never a Schedule VI electronic prescription converted to a computer-generated facsimile.
An emergency waives only the electronic-prescribing requirement; every other prescription requirement continues to apply to the written or oral prescription the emergency permits.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner electronic follow-up after an oral controlled-substance prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: This is the statutory default where the practitioner has received no electronic-prescribing exception.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner written follow-up where the practitioner has received a commissioner's exception
timing_deadlines.consequence: A mailed written prescription must be postmarked within the period.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner follow-up for an oral Schedule II-V prescription issued under an enumerated exception
timing_deadlines.consequence: Seven business days is a longer span than seven calendar days; either a written or an electronic prescription discharges it.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner follow-up after emergency oral Schedule II dispensing
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Seven business days under Massachusetts law, seven days under federal law
timing_deadlines.consequence: The federal seven days is shorter and controls; the document must bear Authorization for Emergency Dispensing.

forms_records.text: The pharmacist immediately reduces the oral prescription to writing on a prescription form with the prescriber, patient, drug, directions, serial number and refill information Massachusetts requires.

The follow-up prescription must indicate on its face that it is issued to document an oral prescription, and on receipt the pharmacy attaches it to the oral prescription it had reduced to writing; the pharmacist's record is incomplete until the two are joined.

A written follow-up must itself satisfy the Massachusetts written-format rules: the practitioner's signature, and either transmission by facsimile or similar technology or a tamper-resistant form consistent with federal Medicaid requirements.
An emergency follow-up prescription bears Authorization for Emergency Dispensing on its face and is attached on receipt to the emergency prescription earlier reduced to writing.

role_duties.duty: Reduce the oral prescription to writing at once, authenticate an unfamiliar prescriber, join the follow-up document to it on arrival, and notify the DEA where an emergency follow-up never comes.
Deliver the follow-up prescription within the period that applies to the route the prescription travelled, in the form that route accepts.

common_traps.text: Calling any transmission outage a Failover waives a follow-up the law still requires; a Failover is Schedule VI by definition, and an outage affecting a Schedule II through V prescription is a different exception entirely.
Reading the three Failover conditions as the whole test misses the definitional limit sitting above them.
Treating every electronic-prescribing exception as something the prescriber holds misreads the list; most attach to the circumstances of the prescription and nobody applies for them.
Quoting seven days and seven business days as though they were the same period gets a follow-up delivered on day nine wrong in one direction or the other.
Looking only for a paper follow-up misses that the regulation accepts a written or an electronic prescription.
Applying the Massachusetts seven business days to an emergency oral Schedule II follow-up ignores the shorter federal seven days that controls it.
Accepting a follow-up on a form no permitted format supports leaves the file resting on an invalid prescription, which may not be filled at all.
